diagrams.title: Diabetes: A1C and fasting blood sugar cut-offs

cloze.text: In the ADPIED process of care: A = Assessment, D = {{c1::Dental hygiene diagnosis}}, P = {{c2::Planning}}, I = {{c3::Implementation}}, E = {{c4::Evaluation}}, D = Documentation.
The ADPIED process of care helps identify {{c1::risk factors}} to aid in the prevention and management of oral diseases.
{{c1::Assessment}} is the first component of the dental hygiene process.
Assessment starts when the clinician {{c1::escorts the patient to the treatment area}} — notice the patient's breathing, physical impairment, appearance, etc.
When taking the medical history and medications, include {{c1::prescription drugs}}, {{c2::over-the-counter drugs}}, and {{c3::supplements}}.
cloze.extra: Obtain past and present medical history, dental history, and medications.

cloze.text: During assessment, consult with the {{c1::physician}} for patients with medical concerns.
During assessment, check {{c1::vital signs}} and assess the patient's physical and mental state.
Assessment includes the extraoral/intraoral examination, assessing the dentition and periodontium, noting abnormalities, and obtaining {{c1::radiographs}} (if necessary).
Risk assessments are performed for {{c1::caries}}, {{c2::periodontal diseases}}, and {{c3::oral cancer}}.

Factors considered in risk assessment include {{c1::fluoride exposure}}, tobacco use, nutrition analysis, {{c2::parafunctional habits}}, lifestyle, age, gender, genetic history, physical disability, etc.
The dental hygiene diagnosis identifies {{c1::current and potential}} oral health problems from the data collected.
A dental hygiene diagnosis is NOT a {{c1::dental diagnosis}} — the actual dental diagnosis is done only by the {{c2::dentist}}.
When writing notes, avoid words that are {{c1::judgmental}} and express emotions.
Planning formulates goals and a sequence of activities based on the patient's {{c1::needs}}, {{c2::values}}, and {{c3::scientific evidence}}.
The treatment plan is formulated by the {{c1::dentist}} (with the hygienist's help); it is presented to the patient to obtain {{c2::informed consent}}.
Failure to provide the highest standard of care (e.g., not referring to a specialist when necessary) is considered {{c1::malpractice (negligence)}}.
In implementation, the hygienist implements the treatment plan that the {{c1::dentist has approved}}.
Implementation includes {{c1::non-surgical periodontal therapy}}, patient education, {{c2::dietary analysis}}, and oral hygiene instructions.
In evaluation, the hygienist reviews and documents the {{c1::outcomes}} of the therapy performed; depending on progress, the {{c2::treatment plan}} may need adjusting.
In a SOAP note, the {{c1::Subjective}} section records what the patient reports: chief complaint, symptoms, medical history, pain level, lifestyle habits (e.g., smoking, home care).
The Subjective (S) section of a SOAP note should always use the {{c1::patient's own words}} if possible.

In a SOAP note, the {{c1::Objective}} section records what the clinician observes or measures: vital signs, clinical findings (e.g., bleeding on probing), radiographic evidence, plaque index, intra/extraoral exam results.

In a SOAP note, the {{c1::Assessment}} section is your clinical interpretation or hygiene status (e.g., gingivitis, moderate periodontitis); it summarizes risk levels and progress from previous visits.
In a SOAP note, the {{c1::Plan}} section records the proposed treatment plan and next steps: education, radiographs needed, debridement, fluoride application, referrals, and recall interval.
The dental hygiene diagnosis provides a basis for the {{c1::dental hygiene care plan}}.

Data for the dental hygiene diagnosis come from the {{c1::patient interview}} (chief complaint, medical history, dental history) and the {{c2::physical assessment}} (vital signs, intra/extraoral exam, periodontal and dental charting).
A dental hygiene diagnostic statement gives the {{c1::problem}}, followed by the {{c2::cause}}.
cloze.extra: Example: heavy biofilm, related to a lack of daily home care at the senior facility.

cloze.text: The dental hygiene diagnosis must be within the scope of practice — e.g., a hygienist cannot diagnose {{c1::caries}} (that is the dentist's scope).
The prognosis is determined {{c1::after the diagnosis}} and {{c2::before the treatment plan is finalized}}.
Prognosis considers individual tooth factors (e.g., {{c1::mobility}}) and overall factors (e.g., {{c2::age}}).
cloze.extra: Details can vary according to the reference.

cloze.text: Good prognosis: control of etiologic factors, adequate biofilm management, {{c1::no clinical attachment loss}}, bleeding on probing {{c2::<10%}}, regular professional care, non-smoker, good diabetes control.

Fair prognosis: control of etiologic factors, adequate biofilm management, bleeding on probing {{c1::>10%}}, attachment loss {{c2::1–4 mm}}, radiographic bone loss {{c3::15–33%}}, probing depths <5 mm, {{c4::Class I}} furcation, no mobility.

Poor prognosis: inadequate plaque control (root anatomy or dexterity), bone loss {{c1::>33%}}, attachment loss {{c2::>5 mm}}, probing depths {{c3::>6 mm}}, vertical bone loss, Class II furcation, {{c4::Class II}} molar mobility, poor diabetes control, tobacco use.

Questionable prognosis: inadequate plaque control with root/dexterity challenges, uncontrolled diabetes, bone loss {{c1::>50%}} + poor crown-to-root ratio, Class II or III furcation, {{c2::Class III}} mobility, root proximity, tobacco use, tooth loss due to periodontitis.
Hopeless prognosis: {{c1::inadequate attachment to support the tooth}}; {{c2::extraction}} recommended.
A dental hygiene care plan includes {{c1::interventions}}, {{c2::expected outcomes}}, {{c3::evaluation methods}}, and a plan for {{c4::re-evaluation}}.
The care plan focuses on the elimination of {{c1::etiologic factors}} (e.g., plaque and calculus removal).
The care plan also includes {{c1::education and behavior modification}}, such as nutritional counseling and smoking cessation.
Oral hygiene instructions (OHI) are customized to the patient's {{c1::abilities and goals}}.
The patient is the {{c1::center of care}} — informed consent must be obtained, and the patient may {{c2::accept or decline}} parts of the proposed plan.
The care plan should reflect the patient's systemic health, risk factors, values, and {{c1::readiness to change}}.

Did you know? In the 1920s–1930s the biannual dental visit gained popularity in the US through {{c1::Ipana toothpaste}} advertisements; in the mid-20th century the {{c2::American Dental Association (ADA)}} began endorsing the six-month recall.
cloze.extra: Canada was influenced by similar marketing and professional endorsements.

cloze.text: The {{c1::initial}} appointment is the first comprehensive visit: full assessment, radiographs, periodontal charting, cancer screening, plaque evaluation, and creation of a personalized care plan.

The {{c1::recall}} appointment is the traditional term for periodic follow-up (reassess, update history, cleaning, radiographs if needed, reinforce home care) — typically every {{c2::6 months}}, varying with individual risk factors.

The {{c1::re-care}} appointment is the patient-centered term for ongoing maintenance visits (all recall components, emphasizing prevention, risk assessment, collaborative care); its interval, based on individual risk, ranges from {{c2::3 to 12 months}}.
The {{c1::re-evaluation}} appointment is a follow-up after initial therapy, typically at {{c2::4–6 weeks}}, to assess healing, re-probe periodontal status, and determine the next phase of care.
Low caries risk (good oral hygiene, no history of periodontal disease): recommended interval {{c1::6–12 months}}.
Moderate caries risk (some risk factors, such as smoking or diabetes): recommended interval {{c1::4–6 months}}.
High caries risk (history of periodontal disease, poor oral hygiene, multiple risk factors): recommended interval {{c1::3–4 months}}.

Recall by periodontal status: healthy/gingivitis every {{c1::6 to 12 months}}; history of periodontitis every {{c2::3 to 4 months}} (maintenance); active periodontitis: re-evaluate 4–6 weeks post-SRP, then every {{c3::3 months}} until stable.
For a patient with angina, have {{c1::nitroglycerin}} (Nitrostat) ready for emergencies.
For a patient with angina, create a stress-free environment; {{c1::morning}} appointments are preferred.
For patients with angina, a history of MI, or hypertension, limit epinephrine to {{c1::0.04 mg}} per appointment = about {{c2::2}} cartridges of 1:100,000.
{{c1::Hypertension}}: increased pressure on the arteries related to the buildup of plaque in the arteries.
For a hypertensive patient, check blood pressure {{c1::before and after}} the procedure.
cloze.extra: The exam uses the AHA 2017 blood-pressure categories.

cloze.text: {{c1::Angioplasty-stent}}: a tiny balloon inserted into the artery to prevent clogging. If {{c2::blood thinners}} are prescribed, heavier and prolonged bleeding can occur.

In {{c1::congestive heart failure (CHF)}}, the heart cannot pump blood effectively, causing inadequate delivery of oxygen and nutrients and fluid buildup (congestion) in the lungs, legs, or other areas.
A patient with CHF may not tolerate a {{c1::supine}} position; avoid {{c2::ultrasonic scalers and air polishers}} if the patient has difficulty breathing.
{{c1::Arrhythmia}}: abnormal electrical conduction to the heart muscles; {{c2::epinephrine}} can worsen the condition.
Ultrasonic or piezoelectric scalers are safe with newer cardiac pacemakers that are {{c1::shielded}}; older models may not be, and {{c2::power scalers}} should be avoided.
In a prosthetic joint replacement, a damaged or diseased joint is replaced with an artificial device, usually made of {{c1::metal, plastic, or ceramic}}.
cloze.extra: The book's heading reads "Artificial (prosthetic) valve", but the text describes a joint.

cloze.text: Prosthetic joint replacements (e.g., hips, knees) {{c1::do not}} routinely require antibiotic premedication for dental procedures, unless the patient's physician specifically recommends it due to a high-risk condition or a history of {{c2::joint infection}}. Patients generally carry documentation for premedication.
cloze.extra: Don't confuse with a prosthetic HEART valve, which IS a high-risk condition requiring antibiotic prophylaxis (AHA 2021).

cloze.text: ADHD (inattentiveness, hyperactivity, impulsiveness, possible learning disability): use the {{c1::"tell, show, do"}} approach and schedule {{c2::short}} appointments.
Alzheimer's disease destroys memory, so patients may not remember to care for their oral health — {{c1::caregiver education}} is important.
Parkinson's disease is related to a lack or impairment of {{c1::dopamine}}.
Parkinson's disease is characterized by rigid movements, {{c1::tremor}}, drooling, and lack of facial expression.

For a Parkinson's patient: suggest a larger toothbrush handle or a {{c1::power toothbrush}} and educate the caregiver; protect the airway and use short appointments; {{c2::stabilize}} instruments to avoid accidents from the tremor.
{{c1::Stroke}}: interrupted or reduced blood flow to the brain causing brain-cell damage, often with sudden weakness or paralysis on one side of the body, difficulty speaking, or facial drooping.
cloze.extra: Manual dexterity may be limited — educate the caregiver and suggest home-care modifications.

cloze.text: {{c1::Dilantin (phenytoin)}}, taken for seizures, can cause gingival hyperplasia.
For a seizure patient, avoid {{c1::bright light in the eyes}} (can trigger a seizure) and make sure the {{c2::medication}} was taken appropriately before the appointment.
Depression: avoid the vasoconstrictor {{c1::levonordefrin}} (used with mepivacaine) in patients taking {{c2::tricyclic antidepressants}} (e.g., Elavil).
Nitrous oxide is contraindicated in patients with {{c1::depression}}, {{c2::alcohol and drug dependency}}, and {{c3::COPD/emphysema}}.
Alcohol and drug dependency: the risk of {{c1::oral cancer}} is higher; avoid {{c2::mouthrinses with alcohol}}.
Anemia (drop in oxygen-carrying hemoglobin): the tongue may lose its {{c1::filiform papillae}}; oral tissues may appear pale or erythematous; patients are often weak and fatigued.
Hemophilia and platelet disorders (abnormal coagulation): patients are at risk for {{c1::spontaneous bleeding}}, prolonged bleeding, and hemorrhages.
For diabetic patients, schedule appointments {{c1::after meals}} and pharmacologic therapy; {{c2::morning}} appointments are preferred.
cloze.extra: Diabetes mellitus: insulin deficiency or abnormality disorder.

cloze.text: Ask a diabetic patient for her last {{c1::HbA1c}} results.
cloze.extra: For patients with diabetes, an HbA1c of less than 7% indicates the condition is well controlled.

cloze.text: Diabetic patients require more frequent {{c1::periodontal maintenance}} and excellent home oral hygiene.
Patients with {{c1::uncontrolled}} diabetes should not be treated until the condition is under control.
Diabetic patients are more susceptible to {{c1::infections}}, including periodontal diseases, and their wound healing is {{c2::poor}}.
Renal disease: patients can have frequent infections, poor healing, and bleeding abnormalities; drugs are excreted more {{c1::slowly}}.
For a dialysis patient, treat the {{c1::day after}} dialysis and take blood pressure on the arm {{c2::opposite}} the dialysis fistula.

Hepatitis (liver inflammation from viruses, toxic substances, etc.): fatigue, nausea, tender joints, and {{c1::jaundice}}; drugs are metabolized more {{c2::slowly}}, so use caution; use standard precautions.

Hypothyroidism (insufficient thyroid hormones): patients can be fatigued and may not tolerate {{c1::cold}}; they can have enlarged thyroid glands, {{c2::delayed}} tooth eruption, small jaw, and malocclusion.
Hyperthyroidism (excessive thyroid hormones): patients can be fatigued and may not tolerate {{c1::heat}}; they can show {{c2::early}} loss of deciduous teeth and early eruption of permanent teeth.
In uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, {{c1::vasoconstrictors}} may be contraindicated due to risk of tachycardia, hypertension, and cardiac arrhythmias.
Acromegaly/gigantism (excessive {{c1::pituitary}} hormones): enlarged maxilla/mandible and {{c2::macroglossia}}.
Cyclic neutropenia: an inherited repeated decrease in neutrophils every {{c1::21 to 27 days}}; start treatment when the neutrophil count is {{c2::normal}}.
cloze.extra: Severe periodontal issues can occur, so frequent appointments are recommended.

cloze.text: Cerebral palsy: a skeletal and muscular disorder caused by a disruption in {{c1::brain development}}; patients may have intellectual, learning and/or physical disability and may need to be treated in a wheelchair.

Spina bifida: a neural tube defect (spine fails to develop and close in the {{c1::first month}} of pregnancy); {{c2::latex allergy}} occurs frequently; often associated with {{c3::folate (vitamin B9)}} deficiency.
cloze.extra: Patient may need to be treated in a wheelchair.

cloze.text: Bell's palsy: {{c1::unilateral}} facial paralysis affecting cranial nerve {{c2::VII (facial)}}. Treat when symptoms resolve (usually spontaneous recovery in {{c3::3 weeks to 6 months}}).
Arthritis: patients can have {{c1::TMJ}} problems; anti-inflammatory medications may prevent {{c2::blood coagulation}}; suggest home-care modifications (bigger toothbrush handle, power toothbrush).
Marfan syndrome (genetic connective-tissue disorder): high palate, crowding, malocclusion; {{c1::heart conditions}} are often present — check medications and the need for premedication.
The hallmark of anorexia nervosa (extremely low body weight) is {{c1::self-starvation}}.
Anorexia and bulimia patients usually present with glossitis, angular cheilitis, bleeding gingiva, and papillae hypertrophy from {{c1::nutritional deficiency}}.
Anorexia nervosa can present with {{c1::lanugo}} (excess fine hair).
Bulimia nervosa (binge eating and purging) is characterized by {{c1::normal or slightly elevated}} body weight.
Purging causes {{c1::perimolysis}} (tooth erosion), especially on the {{c2::lingual surfaces of the maxillary teeth}}.
Bulimia patients can have xerostomia and an enlarged {{c1::parotid}} gland.
Celiac sprue (gluten sensitivity): painful burning tongue (glossitis) and {{c1::atrophy of the papillae}}.
Inhaler use (asthma, COPD) can cause {{c1::oral candidiasis}} and {{c2::xerostomia}} — advise rinsing with water after use.
cloze.extra: Asthma: airway inflammation causing narrowing and excessive mucus. COPD/emphysema: lung diseases that block airflow.

cloze.text: For asthma patients, {{c1::late morning or late afternoon}} appointments are preferred.
Avoid {{c1::ultrasonic scalers and air polishers}} in patients with asthma or COPD/emphysema.
Patients with COPD/emphysema may not tolerate a {{c1::supine}} position.
Addison's disease: hyposecretion of {{c1::cortisol and aldosterone}} by the adrenal glands; patients may have {{c2::skin pigmentation}} (also on oral tissues).
cloze.extra: Provide a stress-free atmosphere — patients may be weak and fatigued.

cloze.text: Tuberculosis (lung infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis): do not treat patients who have {{c1::active or suspected}} TB.

Radiation and chemotherapy patients are more prone to caries, periodontal diseases, and {{c1::oral candidiasis}}; side effects include xerostomia, {{c2::mucositis}}, glossitis, ulcerated mucosa, and NUG.
Cancer-therapy patients should rinse with water or {{c1::baking soda}} after vomiting.
Treat all dental issues {{c1::before}} cancer therapy starts (extracting questionable teeth reduces infection risk); schedule dental treatment {{c2::between}} therapies.

HIV is a viral infection that affects the {{c1::T-lymphocytes}}. It is transmissible only through blood, semen, rectal fluids, vaginal fluids, and breast milk — NOT through {{c2::aerosols, saliva, and sweat}}.
HIV oral signs: candidiasis, {{c1::linear gingival erythema}}, {{c2::Kaposi's sarcoma}} (flat/raised red/purple lesion), {{c3::hairy leukoplakia}}, repetitive herpes simplex lesions, NUG/NUP.
Autism patients are at higher risk for {{c1::caries}}; provide {{c2::repetitive}} encounters in a quiet atmosphere and avoid direct eye contact.
Down syndrome = trisomy {{c1::21}} (an extra chromosome).
cloze.extra: Use the "tell-show-do" approach with positive reinforcement.

cloze.text: Down syndrome oral findings: delayed exfoliation and development, {{c1::fissured tongue}}, {{c2::congenitally missing teeth}}, dry skin/lips, small nasomaxillary complex, altered salivary glands, xerostomia, enamel dysplasia, malocclusion, attrition, {{c3::high palatal vault}}.

For special-needs patients (e.g., Down syndrome), minimize distractions; skeletal cervical anomalies may require {{c1::shorter}} appointments; {{c2::consistency}} (same staff, operatory, appointment time) builds trust and cooperation.
A {{c1::pre-appointment}} (in person or by phone) is helpful to discuss special needs before the first visit.
Special-needs appointments are best scheduled {{c1::early in the day}}, when everyone is alert and waiting time is reduced.
Hypotonia (low muscle tone) causes increased {{c1::range of joint movement}} and motor-function problems — consider it when positioning the patient in the chair.
cloze.extra: Patients may also exhibit spastic movements and/or limited neck movement and pain.

cloze.text: Down syndrome patients may have hearing loss: {{c1::adjust or turn off hearing aids}}, because the sound of some instruments can cause auditory discomfort.

Persons with Down syndrome are generally content and well-natured but can become {{c1::aggressive}} if disoriented or confused; occasionally {{c2::sedation or general anesthesia}} is needed if unmanageable.
In Down syndrome the {{c1::gag reflex}} may be increased, even in the anterior oral cavity (tongue placement and anxiety).
For Down syndrome, consider a {{c1::panoramic radiograph}} to check for congenitally missing teeth — it may be less threatening than individual intraoral images.
cloze.extra: The book says "individual films"; the exam says image receptors/radiographs.

cloze.text: Educating Down syndrome patients with {{c1::visuals}} may work better than auditory teaching; {{c2::rinsing}} may not be appropriate for those with difficulty swallowing or expectorating.

General examination methods: visual observation, palpation, {{c1::auscultation}} (sounds, e.g., TMJ popping), {{c2::olfaction}} (odors, e.g., fruity breath), and {{c3::percussion}} (tapping, e.g., detecting ankylosed teeth).
Face exam: asymmetrical facial paralysis can indicate {{c1::CVA (stroke)}} or Bell's palsy.
Face exam: drooling and lack of expression can indicate {{c1::Parkinson's disease}}.
Face exam: pigmentation can indicate {{c1::Addison's disease}}, skin cancer, etc.
Document extraoral lesions by {{c1::color}}, {{c2::size}}, {{c3::shape}}, and {{c4::texture}}; take a photo and keep it in the records.
Face exam: note any distortion of the facial dimension (e.g., swollen {{c1::parotid glands}}).
Pinpoint pupils ({{c1::miosis}}) can indicate opioid use: heroin/morphine, codeine, fentanyl, methadone, oxycodone.
Dilated pupils ({{c1::mydriasis}}) can indicate {{c2::cocaine}} use.
Yellow sclera can indicate {{c1::jaundice}}.

basic.back: The reason the patient is in the dental office (e.g., whitening, "cleaning")

basic.front: A patient comes in mainly wanting whitening but also has periodontal disease. What do you address first?
basic.back: Her chief complaint (whitening) — acknowledge and discuss it before shifting focus to the periodontal disease.
basic.extra: Board Alert: always address the chief complaint first, even if more serious conditions are present — unless there is an urgent issue like suspected cancer or trauma.

basic.back: A standardized method of clinical documentation used to record patient encounters
The prediction of the treatment outcome, based on the patient's current oral and systemic health, risk factors, and commitment to care
No — it can improve or worsen with changes in patient behavior, systemic health, and treatment response.
basic.extra: Board Alert: definitions of "good," "fair," "poor" vary slightly between textbooks — focus on the clinical indicators, not rigid labels.

basic.back: A structured sequence of services designed to meet the patient's individual needs

basic.front: A patient has diabetes. Per the book's Board Alert, what recall interval would you probably recommend, and why?
basic.back: 3 to 4 months — interval tables are only a general guideline; look at the entire picture and err on the side of caution.
Chest pain or discomfort caused by reduced blood flow (ischemia) to the heart muscle
Death of part of the heart muscle due to a blocked blood supply (heart attack)
A drop in blood pressure when standing up

basic.front: How do you prevent orthostatic hypotension at the end of an appointment?
basic.back: Sit the patient up slowly and let them rest for several minutes before standing or leaving the chair.
A sensory, emotional, or physical sensation that may occur prior to a seizure
basic.extra: Ask seizure patients whether they have an aura.

basic.front: What oral-care advice do you give a patient who purges?
basic.back: Rinse the mouth and avoid brushing immediately after purging; provide fluoride therapy (and, for bulimia, a mouth guard to protect teeth when purging).

basic.front: On the boards, an answer choice suggests contacting the physician to verify information or obtain consent. How should you treat it?
basic.back: It is often the correct choice — confirm with the appropriate source rather than assume or act without proper authorization.
One finger (e.g., touching the hard palate)
A finger and the thumb grab the tissue (e.g., examining the tongue)
All fingers of one hand grasp the tissue (e.g., examining cervical nodes)
Fingers and thumb of both hands applied simultaneously — one inside the mouth, one outside (e.g., floor of the mouth)
Symmetrical structures examined simultaneously (e.g., the TMJ)
Fingers move in a circular motion with slight pressure

typein.question: After a myocardial infarction, how long should non-emergency dental treatment be delayed? (board answer, e.g. "3 months")
typein.extra: Board Alert: emerging evidence supports a shorter interval (4–6 weeks) for medically stable patients cleared by a physician — but unless the question states otherwise, 6 months is the safest answer on US and Canadian boards. Create a stress-free environment.

typein.question: After a stroke, how long should dental treatment be deferred? (e.g. "3 months")
Postpone treatment if the platelet count is below how many per mm³? (write with a comma, e.g. 10,000)
HIV: do not treat when the CD4 cell count is below how many per mm³?
HIV: do not treat when the neutrophil count is below how many per mm³?

match.prompt: Match each appointment type to its description.
pairs: First comprehensive visit; creates the care plan
Traditional term; periodic follow-up, typically every 6 months
Patient-centered maintenance term; 3–12 months by risk
4–6 weeks after initial therapy; re-probe, assess healing

match.prompt: Match each palpation technique to a structure it is used for.

order.prompt: Put the steps of the dental hygiene process of care (ADPIED) in order.
Order the prognosis categories from best to worst.

sort.prompt: Sort each entry into the SOAP section where it belongs.
categories: Patient says her gums bleed when brushing

mcq.question: Which chart entry is written correctly?
options: A. Heavy plaque present because the patient is lazy.
B. Heavy plaque, loss of attachment since the last visit. Risk factors include smoking. Refer to the dentist for a dental diagnosis.
C. Patient is careless about home care, which is frustrating.
D. Patient obviously does not care about her teeth; heavy plaque.
mcq.answer: B. Heavy plaque, loss of attachment since the last visit. Risk factors include smoking. Refer to the dentist for a dental diagnosis.
mcq.explanation: Notes must be objective — state findings and risk factors and refer for the dental diagnosis. The other entries use judgmental, emotional words ("lazy", "careless", "frustrating").

mcq.question: A molar shows 40% radiographic bone loss, 6 mm attachment loss, 7 mm probing depths, a Class II furcation, and Class II mobility. The patient's diabetes is poorly controlled. Which prognosis best fits?
options: A. Fair
B. Poor
C. Questionable
D. Hopeless
mcq.explanation: Bone loss >33%, attachment loss >5 mm, probing depths >6 mm, Class II furcation and Class II molar mobility are the book's "poor" criteria. Questionable would need bone loss >50% with a poor crown-to-root ratio or Class III mobility; fair is only 15–33% bone loss with no mobility.

mcq.question: A patient treated for periodontitis two years ago is now stable with good home care. What periodontal maintenance interval is recommended?
options: A. Every 6–12 months
B. Every 3–4 months
C. Re-evaluate in 4–6 weeks
D. Every 12 months
mcq.explanation: A history of periodontitis calls for 3–4-month maintenance even when stable. 6–12 months is for healthy/gingivitis patients; the 4–6-week re-evaluation follows SRP for ACTIVE periodontitis.

mcq.question: A patient had a myocardial infarction 2 months ago and requests a routine prophylaxis. No other information is given. What is the best course of action?
options: A. Proceed, limiting epinephrine to 0.04 mg
B. Postpone elective treatment until 6 months after the MI
C. Proceed in a morning appointment with nitroglycerin ready
D. Premedicate with antibiotics, then proceed
mcq.answer: B. Postpone elective treatment until 6 months after the MI
mcq.explanation: Unless the question says the patient is medically stable and cleared by the physician, the board answer is to wait 6 months after an MI. The epinephrine limit applies once treatment is appropriate; it does not make treatment at 2 months correct.

mcq.question: A patient had a total knee replacement 3 years ago with no complications and no other medical conditions. Regarding antibiotic premedication before scaling, the hygienist should know that:
options: A. Premedication is required for all prosthetic joints
B. Premedication is required only for the first 2 years
C. Premedication is not routinely required unless her physician recommends it
D. Premedication is required because of bleeding during scaling
mcq.answer: C. Premedication is not routinely required unless her physician recommends it
mcq.explanation: Prosthetic joints do not routinely require antibiotic premedication; it is given only when the physician recommends it for a high-risk condition or a history of joint infection. If in doubt, contacting the physician to verify is often the correct board choice.

mcq.question: A patient with type 2 diabetes reports that her last HbA1c was 9.5%. She has generalized moderate periodontitis. What is the most appropriate action?
options: A. Proceed with SRP; diabetes does not affect periodontal treatment
B. Postpone elective treatment until her diabetes is under control
C. Schedule a late-afternoon appointment before her evening meal
D. Use nitrous oxide to reduce stress
mcq.answer: B. Postpone elective treatment until her diabetes is under control
mcq.explanation: An HbA1c below 7% means well controlled; 9.5% is uncontrolled, and uncontrolled diabetics should not be treated until the condition is controlled. Appointments should be after meals and preferably in the morning — not before a meal.

mcq.question: A normal-weight 19-year-old has smooth erosion on the lingual surfaces of her maxillary teeth, xerostomia, and enlarged parotid glands. Which condition is most likely?
options: A. Anorexia nervosa
B. Bulimia nervosa
C. Celiac sprue
D. Addison's disease
mcq.explanation: Bulimia: normal or slightly elevated body weight, perimolysis on maxillary linguals from purging, xerostomia and enlarged parotids. Anorexia features extremely low body weight (self-starvation, lanugo).

mcq.question: During the assessment, the hygienist notices a fruity odor on the patient's breath. Which examination method is she using?
options: A. Auscultation
B. Olfaction
C. Percussion
D. Palpation
mcq.explanation: Olfaction uses odors (e.g., fruity breath). Auscultation uses sounds (e.g., TMJ popping); percussion is tapping (e.g., ankylosed teeth).
